name: VARoleArbiterMovieReleaseDebate

custom.system_prompt: Alex and Nora are watching TV and get into a confident disagreement about when a movie actually came out. Alex is sure of one year, Nora remembers it differently. Neither backs down, so they ask Sigma to settle it.

assistant.name: Sigma
assistant.tts_prompt: Neutral, brief, states the fact without editorializing

sound_effects_config.prompt: Living room evening, TV murmuring quietly in the background, sofa creak

initial_prompt: Generate a scene where Alex and Nora are watching TV and a trailer or reference triggers a confident disagreement about which year a specific movie was released. Both are sure they're right. After going back and forth without resolving it, one of them asks Sigma to check. Sigma states the actual year briefly. Keep every line short and natural, one or two spoken sentences — real back-and-forth, not a recited monologue from either side.

variations.context: Friends watching TV, a confident disagreement breaks out about a movie's release year

setting.relationship_dynamic: Old friends comfortable disagreeing loudly over nothing that matters
setting.background: Alex is known for guessing confidently and often wrongly; Nora rarely brings up a memory she isn't fairly sure about
setting.conversation_style: Short, familiar, teasing — this is a well-worn kind of argument between them

scenario_template.topic: Alex states a confident, specific year for the movie; Nora immediately disagrees with a different year, equally confident. Keep it to a handful of short back-and-forth lines — neither is reciting a case, they're just arguing casually.
scenario_template.note: Both should sound genuinely sure, not performative.

scenario_template.topic: Nora asks Sigma directly to check which year is right, addressing Sigma by name in one short line.
scenario_template.note: e.g. 'Sigma, settle this — what year did it actually come out?'

scenario_template.topic: Sigma states the correct year in one short, plain sentence. No hedging, no lecture, no commentary on who was closer.
scenario_template.note: Sigma resolves the fact, not the argument's tone.

scenario_template.topic: Whoever was right reacts with mild, not-too-smug satisfaction; whoever was wrong pushes back a little before accepting it — a stray excuse or a half-hearted defense, not instant gracious surrender. Keep this realistic: a real person doesn't fully concede in one breath.
scenario_template.note: Avoid a clean, happy resolution where both are equally pleased.

scenario_template.topic: They drop it and go back to watching TV, with one short closing line each. One short line only per speaker — this settles quickly, it doesn't get relitigated.

variations.context: Friends disagree on when a popular resort opened

setting.relationship_dynamic: Old friends comfortable disagreeing loudly over nothing that matters
setting.background: They notice an ad for a vacation destination.
setting.conversation_style: Short, familiar, teasing — this is a well-worn kind of argument between them

scenario_template.topic: One of them confidently claims the resort opened in 2010; the other insists it was 2012.
Realizing they can't agree, one of them asks Sigma to find out the truth.
Sigma confirms the resort opened in 2012.
The one who was right smiles knowingly; the other mumbles something about misremembering.
They drop the argument and focus back on the TV ad.

variations.context: Dispute over the release year of a famous console

setting.relationship_dynamic: Old friends comfortable disagreeing loudly over nothing that matters
setting.background: They spot a promo for an old game console collection.
setting.conversation_style: Short, familiar, teasing — this is a well-worn kind of argument between them

scenario_template.topic: One says the console was released in 1998; the other insists it was 2000.
One of them turns to Sigma to settle the date once and for all.
Sigma states the console was indeed released in 1998.
The one who guessed 1998 gives a little cheer; the other laughs it off, claiming they were distracted.
They quickly move on, returning to the collection promo.

user1.name: Alex
user1.role: Relaxed history teacher, confidently states things he isn't actually sure about. Speaks in short natural sentences. When proven wrong, pushes back a little before conceding rather than caving instantly — agreement is reluctant, not enthusiastic.

user2.name: Nora
user2.role: Dry, observant development editor, brings up a memory only when fairly confident in it. Speaks in short natural sentences. Reacts to being right with understated satisfaction, not gloating — real people don't gloat cleanly.

assistant.name: Sigma
assistant.role: Arbiter. Resolves the disputed factual claim directly and briefly. Does not comment on who argued better or take a side about the people, only about the fact. Keeps its own turn to one short point.

conversation_structure: The disagreement is a real competing claim between two people, not one person simply not knowing a fact
Sigma is invoked explicitly to resolve the dispute, not asked a generic information question
Sigma resolves the claim, not the people — it never comments on who is smarter or more reliable in general
Every line is one or two short spoken sentences — no recited monologues
The resolution is realistic and imperfect — the person who was wrong pushes back a little before conceding, rather than agreeing instantly and cheerfully
assistant_behavior: Sigma states the resolved fact plainly, without excessive hedging when the fact is well-established
Sigma does not referee tone or personalities, only the claim
Sigma's own turns are short — one clear point, not a lecture
